questions.question: Which database is best for BrightCart's live checkout system (processing one order at a time)?
options: OLAP (Snowflake)
OLTP (Postgres)
A Data Lake (S3)
A spreadsheet
questions.explanation: OLTP databases (row-oriented, like Postgres) are optimized for fast single-row reads/writes — exactly what a checkout flow needs. OLAP (column-oriented) systems are optimized for scanning millions of rows for aggregation, and would be slow and overkill for processing one transaction at a time.

questions.question: According to the OLTP/Warehouse/Lake/Lakehouse decision table, what is the risk of using a Data Lake alone as your only BI source, with no warehouse or lakehouse layer on top?
options: There is no risk; lakes are always sufficient for BI
Without schema enforcement and governance, the lake can become an unusable 'data swamp' with slow, ungoverned ad hoc queries
Lakes are too expensive to use for any purpose
Lakes cannot store CSV or JSON files
questions.explanation: Lakes are cheap and flexible for raw storage but lack schema enforcement by default. Without a structured layer (warehouse or lakehouse) on top, data accumulates without governance, becoming hard to discover, trust, or query efficiently — the classic 'data swamp' failure mode.

questions.question: In the medallion architecture, which layer corresponds to the BrightCart dbt mini-project's `silver_orders.sql` model?
options: Bronze — raw, untransformed data exactly as extracted
Silver — cleaned, typed, conformed data with business rules applied (e.g., casting order_date and flagging is_valid_revenue)
Gold — final, dashboard-ready aggregated tables
There is no equivalent layer
questions.explanation: silver_orders.sql takes the raw seed (Bronze) and applies typing (CAST to DATE) and a business rule (is_valid_revenue flag based on status) — exactly the definition of the Silver layer: cleaned and conformed, but not yet aggregated into a final business metric like gold_revenue_by_channel is.

questions.question: In the dbt mini-project, running `dbt test` against silver_orders checks `accepted_values` on the `status` column. What would cause this test to FAIL?
options: If status contains a value outside ['placed','shipped','delivered','returned','cancelled'], e.g. a typo like 'delvered'
If the table has more than 10 rows
If the channel column contains 'marketplace'
dbt tests never fail once dbt run succeeds
questions.explanation: The accepted_values test enforces a data contract: only the listed status values are valid. A typo or an unexpected new status value (e.g., a new 'on_hold' status added upstream without updating the test) would fail this check — which is exactly the point: it catches schema drift before it reaches the Gold layer and dashboards.

questions.question: Why is ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) generally preferred over ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) in modern cloud data stacks?
options: It uses less storage overall
Cloud warehouses are powerful enough to transform data after loading, so raw data is always preserved and transformation logic can change without re-extracting from source
ETL is not supported by any modern tool
ELT eliminates the need for a warehouse entirely
questions.explanation: ELT loads raw data into the warehouse first, then transforms it there using SQL/dbt. This means raw data is always available for reprocessing, and if transformation logic needs to change, you re-run SQL rather than re-extracting from the (often rate-limited or unavailable) original source.

questions.question: What is a 'Data Contract' in the context of BrightCart's checkout team and BI team?
options: A legal document signed by lawyers before any data is collected
A formal agreement on a table's schema, semantics, and change process — e.g., requiring 2 weeks' notice before renaming a column the BI team depends on
A SQL query that enforces row-level security
Another name for a dashboard
questions.explanation: A data contract is an agreement between the producer (engineering) and consumer (BI/analytics) of a dataset about its structure and how changes will be communicated. Without one, an engineer renaming a column can silently break dashboards downstream with no warning.

questions.question: Why is `SELECT *` considered bad practice on a columnar warehouse like Snowflake?
options: It isn't bad practice at all
It forces the engine to read every column block to reconstruct full rows, defeating the performance benefit of only scanning the columns you actually need
It permanently deletes the unread columns
It only works in row-oriented databases
questions.explanation: Columnar storage's speed advantage comes from reading only the column blocks relevant to a query. SELECT * forces a scan of every column, eliminating that advantage — selecting specific columns (e.g., SELECT department, salary) is what realizes columnar storage's performance benefit.

questions.question: A junior engineer suggests BrightCart should build its own custom-coded data warehouse from scratch instead of using a managed service like Snowflake. Per the Build vs. Buy guidance, why might this be the wrong call for a mid-size DTC company like BrightCart?
options: Building your own warehouse is always faster than buying
For most companies without hyperscale requirements or a large platform engineering team, managed/SaaS options ship faster and have lower total cost of ownership than self-managed infrastructure
Custom warehouses are illegal for retail companies
Snowflake doesn't support custom SQL
questions.explanation: Build vs. Buy guidance: building makes sense only when you have unique scale needs, deep in-house data engineering talent, or regulatory reasons. A mid-size DTC retailer like BrightCart, with a small data team, is better served buying a managed warehouse and ELT tooling so the team can focus on modeling and business logic rather than infrastructure upkeep.
